name: Pi attenuator
seoDesc: Pi attenuator: work out attenuation (in decibels) from the impedance factor and the source impedance. A free other calculator with the formula, units and…
summary: Supply the impedance factor, the source impedance and the load impedance and the Pi attenuator calculator solves for attenuation (in decibels). That makes it useful for whatever you happen to be working on. The panel waits for the button. Edit a field, press Calculate, and compare — one input at a time is enough to see what drives the answer.

sections.title: How does the Pi attenuator calculator work?
sections.html:
The Pi attenuator calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports attenuation (in decibels) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the circuit type); then you type in the impedance factor (K), the source impedance (Zₛ) and the load impedance (ZL).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• Pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as equal impedances and unequal impedances. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A plain number with no unit attached.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in ohms. The unit chip switches it to any of the 5 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in ohms. The unit chip switches it to any of the 5 supported units.

1 field on this form is a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Pi attenuator calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Attenuation (in decibels)=20 × the natural log of (impedance factor (K)) ÷ the natural log of (10)
Impedance (Z₀)=resistor 1 (R₁) × (impedance factor (K) − 1) ÷ (impedance factor (K) + 1)
Impedance (Z₀)=2 × resistor 2 (R₂) × impedance factor (K) ÷ ((impedance factor (K) ^ 2) − 1)
Resistor 1 (R₁)=2 × resistor 2 (R₂) × impedance factor (K) ÷ ((impedance factor (K) ^ 2) − 2 × impedance factor (K) + 1)
Resistor 1 (R₁)=(source impedance (Zₛ) × ((impedance factor (K) ^ 2) − 1) ÷ ((impedance factor (K) ^ 2) − 2 × impedance factor (K) × the square root of (source impedance (Zₛ) ÷ load impedance (ZL)) + 1))
Resistor 2 (R₂)=((1 ÷ 2) × the square root of (load impedance (ZL) × source impedance (Zₛ)) × ((impedance factor (K) ^ 2) − 1) ÷ impedance factor (K))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Circuit type set to Equal impedances and Impedance factor (K) = 10. The calculator returns Attenuation (in decibels) = 20 ​..

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Attenuation (in decibels) = 20 ​. should be roughly the size you expected from Circuit type set to Equal impedances and Impedance factor (K) = 10.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Decibels, opening in decibels (multiplied by 10)
  • Resistance – ohms, opening in ohms
  • Resistance – ohms, opening in ohms
  • Resistance – ohms, opening in ohms
  • Resistance – ohms, opening in ohms
  • Resistance – ohms, opening in ohms
  • Resistance – ohms, opening in ohms

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Pi attenuator calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the impedance factor, the source impedance and the load impedance — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Pi attenuator calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns attenuation (in decibels), derived from the impedance factor, the source impedance and the load impedance. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Pi attenuator calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the impedance factor, the source impedance and the load impedance, which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter attenuation (in decibels) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Attenuation (in decibels) opens in decibels (multiplied by 10) and the chip beside it offers 3 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Attenuation (in decibels) = 20 ​.. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Pi attenuator calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
